lesson.title: Histograms: Grouping Numbers Into Bars
lesson.summary: A histogram displays the distribution of a quantitative variable by grouping values into equal width, touching bars, trading exact individual values for a clear picture of the overall pattern.
lesson.body:
A histogram displays the distribution of a quantitative variable by dividing the range of the data into equal width intervals, called bins or classes, and drawing a bar over each bin whose height represents the frequency, or relative frequency, of data values that fall inside that interval. Unlike a bar graph's separated bars for distinct categories, a histogram's bars touch each other directly, with no gaps, because the horizontal axis represents a single continuous numeric scale where each bin picks up exactly where the previous one leaves off.

Building a histogram starts by choosing bin boundaries that cover the full range of the data without overlapping, then counting how many data values fall into each bin, essentially building a frequency table where the rows are intervals instead of single values. The height of each bar is drawn to match that bin's count, or its relative frequency if you prefer a proportion scale, and because every bin has the same width, the bars can be compared fairly just by looking at their heights.

Return to the 12 test scores used for the stemplot: 62, 67, 71, 73, 74, 78, 81, 85, 85, 89, 92, 95. Using bins of width 10, starting at 60, gives four intervals: 60 up to but not including 70, 70 up to 80, 80 up to 90, and 90 up to 100. Sorting the scores into these bins: 60 to 70 contains 62 and 67, a count of 2. 70 to 80 contains 71, 73, 74, and 78, a count of 4. 80 to 90 contains 81, 85, 85, and 89, a count of 4. 90 to 100 contains 92 and 95, a count of 2. Checking the total: 2 plus 4 plus 4 plus 2 equals 12, matching all 12 scores.

A histogram of this data would show four touching bars of heights 2, 4, 4, and 2 across the four intervals, immediately revealing that most scores cluster in the middle two bins, the 70s and 80s, while fewer scores fall in the lowest and highest bins. This is exactly the same information the stemplot organized by stems and leaves, but the histogram trades the ability to read back every exact last digit for a cleaner visual sense of the overall pattern, which becomes especially valuable once a data set has too many distinct values for a dotplot or stemplot to handle cleanly.

The bin width chosen for a histogram is not fixed by any rule of the data itself. It is a decision the person building the graph must make, and different reasonable choices of bin width can make the same underlying data look noticeably different, sometimes hiding real structure and sometimes exaggerating random noise. That decision, and the trade offs involved in making it well, is the exact subject of the next section, choosing bin width, which builds directly on the histogram introduced here.

Just as with a bar graph, a histogram can be drawn using relative frequency instead of raw frequency on the vertical axis, which is especially useful when comparing two histograms built from data sets of different total sizes, since it rescales each bar to represent a proportion of its own data set rather than a raw count. The overall shape of the histogram, where the bars stand tall and where they stay short, is exactly the same either way, only the labeling and scale of the vertical axis changes.
